newsitem.title: USA: American Quakers nominate Carter for Nobel prize.
newsitem.headline: American Quakers nominate Carter for Nobel prize.

text.p: The American service arm of the Quakers has nominated former U.S. President Jimmy Carter for this year's Nobel Peace Prize, the group said on Tuesday.

The American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), which itself won the peace prize in 1947 for its work among the victims of the Second World War, said Carter deserved to be recognised for his worldwide efforts at promoting peace and democracy.
The Quakers, known formally as the Religious Society of Friends, also emphasised the spiritual underpinnings of the endeavours pursued by the former president, who is a devout Southern Baptist.

Separately, Carter also was nominated by Irwin Abrams, an authority on the Nobel Peace Prize who worked for the AFSC in Europe after the war. Abrams said he was eligible to nominate the former president by virtue of his position as a professor emeritus of history at Antioch University in Ohio.
"Carter's work reflects the Quaker concerns for mutuality and respect for all persons," AFSC executive director Kara Newell said in a statement.
"President Carter continues to demonstrate how a former president can make a unique contribution to ending armed conflicts and building the foundation for a peaceful world."

The Quaker statement said Carter should be recognised particularly for his widely publicised peacemaking missions to North Korea, Bosnia and Haiti; his promotion of democratic elections for Palestinians and Nicaraguans; and his attempts to solve the conflict between the Hutu and Tutsi peoples of the Great Lakes region of Africa.

"It is a great honour for President Carter to be nominated," said Deanna Congileo, spokeswoman for the Atlanta-based Carter Centre, which serves as the global headquarters for the former president's activities.
President Carter was last nominated by the Quakers in 1991.

As a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the AFSC said it was entitled to nominate individuals or groups for the award. In years past, Martin Luther King, Dag Hammarskjold and Sir John Boyd Orr have received the prize in the same year that they were nominated by the Quaker committee.
South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu won the Nobel prize in 1984 after being nominated by the AFSC in 1981 and 1982.
